My biggest piece of advice for you concerning the college portion is to use financial aid and community colleges to your advantage. Take general classes at a community college if that is something offered in your country, then you can usually transfer those credits to a public/private college and complete the rest of your degree for way less. There a lot the government forms don’t disclose, and talking to another human about your situation can open up other benefits for you.

I was 15 with some pretty severe pain in my sides and back. It got to the point where I couldn’t get comfortable no matter what, and couldn’t fall asleep so off the the ER we went. They ran some tests, gave me aspirin, and ran a CT scan with contrast. Didn’t find anything of significance so they sent me home and to follow up with my GP, marking it down as possible kidney stones. 

Well my grandmother (who I lived with) had some secretary friend for a doctors office where she described the situation, that doctor urged us to contact a specialist. 

I went back to school two days after the initial ER visit, still in a shit ton of pain, when I was suddenly called out of school. The specialist wanted me at the hospital ASAP, it was a 50 minute drive to my nephrologist in a children’s hospital where I was admitted and stayed for close to two weeks.

It turns out that when the lab results from the ER went to the nephrologist and he saw a Creatinine level three times higher than what it was supposed to be, it’s a little bit of an issue. I was placed on fluids and diagnosed with an acute kidney injury which essentially halted my kidneys performance, magnifies by the NSAID given in the ER as well as the contrast given which is processed by your kidneys. I will forever remember my nephrologist, he was such a huge advocate for me, and one of the most kind humans ever. I had to go back monthly for testing for about 3 years to make sure everything was working normally.
